questions.prompt: Glow-in-the-dark stickers are an example of fluorescence.
questions.explanation: Glow-in-the-dark materials are an example of phosphorescence (which slowly releases stored energy over time), not fluorescence (which ceases almost immediately when the excitation light stops).

questions.prompt: Explain why every element produces its own unique line spectrum, and how astronomers use this to find out which elements are present in a distant star.
questions.modelAnswer: Each element has unique electron energy levels, emitting or absorbing specific wavelengths of light (a spectral fingerprint). Astronomers compare the lines in a star's spectrum against known laboratory spectra of elements to identify which elements are present in the star.
questions.explanation: Because energy levels are quantised and unique to each atom's nuclear charge and electron configuration, spectral transitions act like a chemical barcode.

questions.prompt: As the electron in hydrogen moves to higher values of n, which quantity INCREASES?
questions.explanation: As n increases, the electron moves farther from the nucleus; its speed and kinetic energy decrease, while its total energy En = -13.6/n² eV increases (becomes less negative, approaching 0 eV at n = ∞).

questions.prompt: Find the wavelength (in nm) of the first line of the Lyman series (n = 2 → 1) of hydrogen.
The 2s orbital is smaller than the 1s orbital.
questions.explanation: The 2s orbital has a higher principal quantum number (n = 2) and is larger in size and higher in energy than the 1s orbital (n = 1).

questions.prompt: Please Confirm!
choices: I confirm that I have read, understood, and agree to abide by all exam rules and academic integrity policies..
I confirm that I have read, understood, and agree to abide by all exam rules and academic integrity policies.
questions.explanation: Academic integrity confirmation. Either option is accepted.

questions.prompt: Find the energy of the electron in the n = 4 level of He⁺ (Z = 2), in eV (include the sign).
Why do the electrons in the gold atoms have almost no effect on the paths of the α particles?
choices: Electrons move too slowly to meet the α particles
Electrons are far too light to deflect the much heavier α particles
questions.explanation: Alpha particles are approximately 7300 times more massive than electrons. Because of this enormous mass difference, collisions with electrons produce virtually no noticeable deflection of the alpha particles.

questions.prompt: Which element was discovered in the spectrum of the Sun before it was found on Earth?
questions.explanation: Helium was first detected by astronomers analyzing solar emission lines during an 1868 eclipse and named after Helios (Greek god of the Sun) before it was isolated on Earth.

questions.prompt: The energy levels of hydrogen get closer together as n increases.
questions.explanation: The energy difference ΔE = 13.6(1/n² - 1/(n+1)²) decreases rapidly as n increases, crowding closer together toward 0 eV as n approaches infinity.

questions.prompt: Match each item with its description.

pairs.right: Tiny, heavy, positive centre of the atom
Packet of light energy, E = hf

distractors: Neutral particle with the mass of an electron
questions.explanation: Electron: negative charge (-e) and very small mass. Nucleus: dense, positively charged core. Photon: quantum of light with energy E = hf. Alpha particle: helium-4 nucleus with charge +2e.

questions.prompt: Which equation is Bohr's quantum condition for the allowed orbits?
questions.explanation: Bohr postulated that orbital angular momentum is quantised in integral multiples of h/(2π): L = mvr = nh/(2π).

questions.prompt: What does the word LASER stand for?
choices: Light Absorption by Stimulated Emission of Rays
Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation
Light Amplification by Spontaneous Emission of Radiation
questions.explanation: LASER stands for Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation.

questions.prompt: A 1 mW laser pointer can permanently damage the eye, but looking briefly at a 60 W light bulb does not. Using the properties of laser light, explain why. Include a calculation or estimate to support your argument.
questions.modelAnswer: A laser emits a coherent, parallel beam that the eye's lens focuses onto a tiny retinal spot (A ≈ 10⁻⁸ m²), creating a dangerous intensity (I = P/A = 0.001 W / 10⁻⁸ m² = 10⁵ W/m²). A 60 W bulb emits incoherent light in all directions, so at 1 m away its intensity spreads over a sphere (A = 4πr² ≈ 12.6 m²), yielding only I ≈ 4.8 W/m².
questions.explanation: The extreme directionality and spatial coherence of a laser beam allows it to be focused to a diffraction-limited spot on the retina, yielding dangerously high power densities.

questions.prompt: What is the shape of an s orbital?
questions.explanation: An s orbital has azimuthal quantum number l = 0, which corresponds to a spherically symmetric probability distribution.

questions.prompt: Which sub-shell is filled immediately after 4s?
questions.explanation: According to the Aufbau principle / Madelung rule, sub-shells fill in order of increasing (n + l). For 4s, n + l = 4 + 0 = 4. The next lowest is 3d with n + l = 3 + 2 = 5.

questions.prompt: Which photon can be absorbed by the hydrogen atom to go to an excited state.
questions.explanation: A ground-state hydrogen atom (n = 1, E₁ = -13.6 eV) can only absorb a photon whose energy precisely matches an energy level difference. For n = 2 (E₂ = -3.4 eV), ΔE = -3.4 - (-13.6) = 10.2 eV.

questions.prompt: Match the suitable pairs (Isotopes of Hydrogen)
questions.explanation: Hydrogen-1 (protium): 1 proton, 0 neutrons. Hydrogen-2 (deuterium): 1 proton, 1 neutron. Hydrogen-3 (tritium): 1 proton, 2 neutrons.

questions.prompt: Match each quantum number with what it describes.

pairs.right: Orientation of the orbital in space
Size and energy of the shell

questions.explanation: n designates shell size/energy; l designates orbital angular momentum/shape; ml designates orbital orientation in space; ms designates intrinsic electron spin.

questions.prompt: For n = 3, which values of l are allowed?
questions.explanation: For any principal quantum number n, the azimuthal quantum number l can take integer values from 0 up to n - 1. For n = 3, l = 0 (s), 1 (p), 2 (d).

questions.prompt: An electron with 11.0 eV of kinetic energy collides with a ground-state hydrogen atom. What can happen?
choices: Nothing, because 11.0 eV matches no gap
It can excite the atom to n = 2 and keep 0.8 eV
It can excite the atom to n = 3
questions.explanation: Unlike photons, colliding electrons can undergo inelastic scattering and transfer part of their kinetic energy. Excitations from n = 1 to n = 2 requires 10.2 eV. Since 11.0 eV > 10.2 eV (and < 12.09 eV for n = 3), the electron excites the atom to n = 2 and keeps 11.0 - 10.2 = 0.8 eV.

questions.prompt: A p sub-shell contains three orbitals.
questions.explanation: For a p sub-shell (l = 1), ml has 2l + 1 = 3 allowed values (-1, 0, +1), corresponding to three mutually perpendicular orbitals (px, py, pz).

questions.prompt: Ground-state hydrogen is bombarded with electrons of 12.8 eV. Find the LONGEST wavelength of light (in nm) that the gas can then emit.
questions.explanation: Electrons with 12.8 eV can excite hydrogen up to n = 4 (requires 12.75 eV). De-excitation pathways include the transition from n = 3 to n = 2 in the Balmer series, which emits the H-α line at 656.1 nm (or 656 nm).

questions.prompt: Explain why light from an ordinary bulb is incoherent while laser light is coherent. Refer to spontaneous and stimulated emission in your answer.
questions.modelAnswer: An ordinary bulb produces light via spontaneous emission, where excited atoms release photons independently at random times, directions, phases, and wavelengths (incoherent). A laser uses stimulated emission, where an incoming photon triggers an excited atom to emit an identical photon with the exact same wavelength, phase, and direction (coherent).
questions.explanation: Spontaneous emission produces randomly phased wave packets with low coherence, while stimulated emission clones identical photons that are in phase with one another.

questions.prompt: What is the maximum number of electrons that the n = 4 shell can hold?
questions.explanation: The maximum capacity of an electron shell is 2n². For n = 4: 2(4²) = 2(16) = 32 electrons.

questions.prompt: If the speed of an electron doubles, its de Broglie wavelength halves.
questions.explanation: The de Broglie wavelength is given by λ = h / (mv). Since λ is inversely proportional to velocity v, doubling the speed halves the wavelength.

questions.prompt: Which set of quantum numbers (n, l, m_l, m_s) is NOT allowed?
questions.explanation: The azimuthal quantum number l is restricted to 0 ≤ l ≤ n - 1. When n = 2, l can only be 0 or 1. Hence, (2, 2, 0, +1/2) is not permitted.

questions.prompt: Why was the gold-foil apparatus kept in a vacuum?
choices: So that air molecules would not stop or scatter the α particles
So that the α particles would travel faster than light
So that the gold foil would not melt
So that the electrons could leave the gold atoms
questions.explanation: Alpha particles strongly ionise matter and have very short range in air (only a few centimetres). A vacuum ensures that observed scattering is due only to the gold atoms.

questions.prompt: Two lasers have the same power. Laser A emits 400 nm light and laser B emits 800 nm light. Which statement is correct?
choices: Both emit the same number of photons per second
Laser A emits four times as many photons per second
Laser B emits twice as many photons per second as laser A
Laser A emits twice as many photons per second as laser B
questions.explanation: Each photon has energy E = hc/λ. An 800 nm photon has half the energy of a 400 nm photon. For both lasers to emit the same total power (energy per second), laser B must emit twice as many photons per second.

questions.prompt: What colour is the light from a helium–neon laser?
questions.explanation: The most common emission line of a helium-neon laser is at 632.8 nm (roughly 633 nm), which is vibrant red visible light.

questions.prompt: Match the suitable pairs (Spectra Types)
questions.explanation: Continuous Spectrum corresponds to A, Absorption Spectrum corresponds to C, and Emission Spectrum corresponds to B.

questions.prompt: Roughly how large is a whole atom?
questions.explanation: Typical atomic diameters are on the order of 10⁻¹⁰ m (0.1 nm or 1 Å). In contrast, the nucleus is about 10⁻¹⁵ m.

questions.prompt: How much energy is needed to ionise a hydrogen atom that is already in the n = 2 level?
questions.explanation: In the n = 2 state, the electron's binding energy is E₂ = -13.6/2² = -3.4 eV. Ionisation requires providing enough energy to lift the electron to n = ∞ (0 eV): E_ion = 0 - (-3.4 eV) = 3.4 eV.
